arXiv:1010.3050v2 [math.DS] 02 Mar 2011

Persistence and permanence of mass-action and power-law dynamical systems

Gheorghe Craciun ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Department of Biomolecular Chemistry, University of Wisconsin-Madison (craciun@math.wisc.edu).    Fedor Nazarov ††thanks: Department of Mathematics, University of Wisconsin-Madison (nazarov@math.wisc.edu).    Casian Pantea ††thanks: Department of Mathematics and Department of Biomolecular Chemistry, University of Wisconsin-Madison (pantea@math.wisc.edu).
Abstract

Persistence and permanence are properties of dynamical systems that describe the long-term behavior of the solutions, and in particular specify whether positive solutions approach the boundary of the positive orthant. Mass-action systems (or more generally power-law systems) are very common in chemistry, biology, and engineering, and are often used to describe the dynamics in interaction networks. We prove that two-species mass-action systems derived from weakly reversible networks are both persistent and permanent, for any values of the reaction rate parameters. Moreover, we prove that a larger class of networks, called endotactic networks, also give rise to permanent systems, even if we allow the reaction rate parameters to vary in time. These results also apply to power-law systems and other nonlinear dynamical systems. In addition, ideas behind these results allow us to prove the Global Attractor Conjecture for three-species systems.

keywords
persistence, permanence, global attractor conjecture, mass-action kinetics, power-law systems, biochemical networks, interaction networks

1 Introduction

Determining qualitative properties of solutions of dynamical systems arising from nonlinear interactions is generally a daunting task. However, a relevant mathematical theory that pertains to biochemical interactions obeying mass-action kinetics has been developed over the last 40 years, starting with the seminal work of Fritz Horn, Roy Jackson and Martin Feinberg, [8, 11, 12]. Generally termed “Chemical Reaction Network Theory”, this theory establishes qualitative results that describe the surprisingly stable dynamic behavior of large classes of mass-action systems, independently of the values of the reaction rate parameters [8]. This fact is especially useful since the exact values of the system parameters are usually unknown.

Here we focus on the properties of persistence and permanence for mass-action systems, and the more general power-law systems. A dynamical system on ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} is called persistent if no trajectory that starts in the positive orthant has an ω\omega-limit point on the boundary of ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}, and is called permanent if all trajectories that start in the positive orthant eventually enter a compact subset of ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n}. Persistence and permanence are important in understanding properties of biochemical networks (e.g., will each chemical species be available indefinitely in the future), and also in ecology (e.g., will a species become extinct in an ecosystem), and in the dynamics of infectious diseases (e.g., will an infection die off, or will it infect the whole population).

In the context of biochemical networks we formulate the following conjecture:

Persistence Conjecture. Any weakly reversible mass-action system is persistent.

Here a weakly reversible mass-action system is one for which its directed reaction graph has the property that each of its connected components is strongly connected11 1 See Definition 5. [8]. A version of this conjecture was first mentioned in [9]22 2 The version in [9] only required that no positive trajectory converges to a boundary point; we conjecture that even more is true: no positive trajectory has an ω\omega-limit point on the boundary..

In this paper we prove the Persistence Conjecture for two-species networks. Moreover, we introduce a new class of networks called endotactic networks, which contains the class of weakly reversible networks, and we show that endotactic two-species κ\kappa-variable mass action systems are permanent (Theorem 19).

For two-species systems, this is a stronger statement than the Persistence Conjecture, in several ways. First, permanence here means that there is a compact set KK in the interior of the positive orthant such that all forward trajectories of positive initial condition end up in KK. Therefore, our result implies both strong persistence and uniform boundedness of trajectories for two-species κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems. Second, our mass-action system is κ\kappa-variable, meaning that the reaction rate constants are allowed to vary within a compact subset of (0,∞)(0,\infty). This makes our result applicable to a larger class of kinetics than just mass-action. Finally, the class of endotactic networks, explained in detail in section 4 strictly contains the class of weakly reversible networks. We conjecture that endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass action systems are permanent for any number of species.

On the other hand, note that the Persistence Conjecture for three or more species remains open.

The Persistence Conjecture is also strongly related to the Global Attractor Conjecture, which was first stated over 35 years ago [11], and is one of the main open questions in Chemical Reaction Network Theory. It is concerned with the global asymptotic stability of positive equilibria for the class of “complex-balanced” [12, 11, 8, 9] mass-action systems. It is known that such systems admit a unique positive equilibrium cΣc_{\Sigma} within each stoichiometric compatibility class33 3 A stoichiometric compatibility class is a minimal linear invariant subset; see Definition 2. Σ\Sigma. Moreover, each such equilibrium admits a strict Lyapunov function and therefore cΣc_{\Sigma} is locally asymptotically stable with respect to Σ{\Sigma} [8, 12]. However, the existence of this Lyapunov function does not guarantee that cΣc_{\Sigma} is a global attractor, which is the object of the following conjecture:

Global Attractor Conjecture. Given a complex-balanced mass-action system and any of its stoichiometric compatibility classes Σ{\Sigma}, the positive equilibrium point cΣc_{\Sigma} is a global attractor on i​n​t​(Σ).int({\Sigma}).

Trajectories of complex-balanced mass-action systems must converge to the set of equilibria [18]. This makes the Global Attractor Conjecture equivalent to showing that any complex-balanced system is persistent, i.e. no trajectory with positive initial condition gets arbitrarily close to the boundary of the positive orthant. Therefore, since a complex-balanced mass-action system is necessarily weakly reversible [8], a proof of the Persistence Conjecture would imply the Global Attractor Conjecture. In general, both conjectures are still open; the Persistence Conjecture has not been proved previously in any dimension, but recent developments have been achieved towards a proof of the Global Attractor Conjecture. For instance, Anderson [1] and Craciun, Dickenstein, Shiu and Sturmfels [5] showed that vertices of the stoichiometric compatibility class Σ\Sigma cannot be ω\omega-limit points and that the Global Attractor Conjecture is true for a class of systems with two-dimensional stoichiometric compatibility classes. Anderson and Shiu proved that for a weakly reversible mass-action system, the trajectories that originate in the interior of Σ\Sigma are “repelled” away from the codimension-one faces of Σ\Sigma. This allowed them to prove that the Global Attractor Conjecture is true if the stoichiometric compatibility class is two-dimensional [2].

2 Definitions and notation

A chemical reaction network is usually given by a finite list of reactions that involve a finite set of chemical species. For example, a reaction network involving two species A1A_{1} and A2A_{2} is given in Figure 1.

We define the functions cA1​(t)c_{A_{1}}(t) and cA2​(t)c_{A_{2}}(t) to be the molar concentrations of species A1,A2A_{1},A_{2} at time tt. The changes in the concentrations are dictated by the chemical reactions in the network; for instance, whenever the reaction A1+A2→2​A1A_{1}+A_{2}\to 2A_{1} occurs, the net gain is a molecule of A1A_{1}, whereas one molecule of A2A_{2} is lost.

2.1 Chemical reaction networks

Here we recall some standard terminology of Chemical Reaction Network Theory (see [8, 12]). In what follows the set of nonnegative, respectively strictly positive real numbers are denoted by ℝ≥0\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0} and ℝ>0\mathbb{R}_{>0} . For any integer n>1n>1 we call ℝ>0n\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{n} the positive orthant and ℝ≥0n\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n} the closed positive orthant. For an arbitrary finite set II we denote by ℤ≥0I{\mathbb{Z}}_{\geq 0}^{I} and ℝ≥0I{\mathbb{R}}_{\geq 0}^{I} the set of all formal sums α=∑i∈Iαi​i\alpha=\displaystyle\sum_{i\in I}\alpha_{i}i where αi\alpha_{i} are nonnegative integers, respectively reals. The support of an element α∈ℝI\alpha\in\mathbb{R}^{I} is s​u​p​p​(α)={i∈I:αi≠0}.supp(\alpha)=\{i\in I:\alpha_{i}\neq 0\}.

Definition 1.

A chemical reaction network is a triple (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)(\mathcal{S},\mathcal{C},\mathcal{R}), where 𝒮\mathcal{S} is the set of chemical species, 𝒞⊆ℤ≥0𝒮\mathcal{C}\subseteq\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{\mathcal{S}} is the set of complexes (i.e., the objects on left or right side of the reaction arrows), and ℛ\mathcal{R} is a relation on 𝒞\mathcal{C}, denoted P→P′P\to P^{\prime}, representing the set of reactions in the network. Here PP is called the source complex and P′P^{\prime} is called the target complex of the reaction P→P′.P\to P^{\prime}. Moreover, the set ℛ\mathcal{R} must satisfy the following three conditions: it cannot contain elements of the form P→PP\to P; for any P∈𝒞P\in\mathcal{C} there exists some P′∈𝒞P^{\prime}\in\mathcal{C} such that either P→P′P\to P^{\prime} or P′→PP^{\prime}\to P; and the union of the supports of all P∈𝒞P\in\mathcal{C} is 𝒮\mathcal{S}.

The second condition in Definition 1 guarantees that each complex appears in at least one reaction, and the third condition assures that each species appears in at least one complex. For the reaction network in Figure 1, the set of species is 𝒮={A1,A2}\mathcal{S}=\{A_{1},A_{2}\}, the set of complexes is 𝒞={2​A1,A1+A2,2​A2}\mathcal{C}=\{2A_{1},A_{1}+A_{2},2A_{2}\} and the set of reactions is ℛ={2A1⇌A1+A2,A1+A2⇌2A2,2A2⇌2A1}\mathcal{R}=\{2A_{1}\rightleftharpoons A_{1}+A_{2},A_{1}+A_{2}\rightleftharpoons 2A_{2},2A_{2}\rightleftharpoons 2A_{1}\}, which consists of 6 reactions, represented as three reversible reactions. For convenience, we refer to a chemical reaction network by specifying ℛ\mathcal{R} only, since it encompasses all the information about the network.

By a slight abuse of notation we may view all complexes as (column) vectors of dimension equal to the number of elements of 𝒮\mathcal{S}, via an identification given by a fixed ordering of the species. To exemplify, the complexes in Figure 1 are 2​A1=[20]2A_{1}=\begin{bmatrix}2\\ 0\\ \end{bmatrix}, A1+A2=[11]A_{1}+A_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}1\\ 1\\ \end{bmatrix}, and 2​A2=[02]2A_{2}=\begin{bmatrix}0\\ 2\\ \end{bmatrix}. For any reaction P→P′P\to P^{\prime} we may thus consider the vector P′−P,P^{\prime}-P, called the reaction vector of P→P′.P\to P^{\prime}.

Definition 2.

The stoichiometric subspace SS of ℛ\cal R is defined as

S=s​p​a​n​{P′−P∣P→P′∈ℛ}.S=span\{P^{\prime}-P\mid P\to P^{\prime}\in\cal R\}.

Suppose ℛ\cal R has dd species, fix an order among them and c⁡(t)∈ℝ𝒮≡ℝdc(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{\cal S}\equiv\mathbb{R}^{d} denote the vector of molar species concentrations at time tt. We refer to c⁡(t)c(t) as the concentration vector of ℛ\cal R at tt. As we will see soon, for all t≥0,t\geq 0, the concentration vector c⁡(t)c(t) is constrained to the stoichiometric compatibility class of c⁡(0),c(0), a special polytope in ℝ≥0d,\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}, defined below.

Definition 3.

Let c0∈ℝd.c^{0}\in\mathbb{R}^{d}. The polytope (c0+S)∩ℝ≥0d(c^{0}+S)\cap\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d} is called the stoichiometric compatibility class of c0.c^{0}.

The reaction network ℛ\cal R can be viewed as a directed graph whose vertices are given by complexes and whose edges correspond to reactions of ℛ\cal R. The connected components of this graph are called linkage classes of ℛ.\cal R.

Definition 4.

A reaction network ℛ\cal R is called reversible if P′→P∈ℛP^{\prime}\to P\in\cal R whenever P→P′∈ℛ.P\to P^{\prime}\in\cal R.

Definition 5.

A reaction network ℛ\cal R is called weakly reversible if its associated directed graph has strongly connected components.

2.2 κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems

Throughout this paper, the differential equations that govern the evolution of the concentration vector c⁡(t)c(t) will be given by κ\kappa-variable mass-action kinetics. The next definition clarifies this notion; to state it, we need the following notation: given two vectors u=∑s∈𝒮us​su=\displaystyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}u_{s}s and v=∑s∈𝒮vs​sv=\displaystyle\sum_{s\in\mathcal{S}}v_{s}s in ℝ≥0𝒮\mathbb{R}^{\mathcal{S}}_{\geq 0}, we denote uv=∏s∈𝒮(us)vsu^{v}=\displaystyle\prod_{s\in\mathcal{S}}(u_{s})^{v_{s}}, with the convention 00=10^{0}=1.

Definition 6.

A κ\kappa-variable mass-action system is a quadruple (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ,κ)({\cal S},{\cal C},{\cal R},\kappa) where (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ)({\cal S},{\cal C},{\cal R}) is a reaction network and κ:ℝ≥0→(η,1/η)ℛ\kappa:\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}\to(\eta,1/\eta)^{\cal R} for some η<1\eta<1 is a piecewise differentiable function called the rate constants function. Given the initial condition c⁡(0)=c0∈ℝ≥0d,c(0)=c^{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}, the concentration vector c⁡(t)c(t) is the solution of the κ\kappa-variable mass-action ODE system

c˙​(t)=∑P→P′κP→P′​(t)​c​(t)P​(P′−P).\dot{c}(t)=\sum_{P\to P^{\prime}}\kappa_{P\to P^{\prime}}(t)c(t)^{P}(P^{\prime}-P). (1)

The κ\kappa-variable mass-action kinetics is a natural generalization of the widely used mass-action kinetics, where the rate constant functions κ⁡(⋅)\kappa(\cdot) are simply positive constants. Therefore any results we prove for κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems are also true for mass-action systems.

Note that integration of (1) yields

c⁡(t)=c0+∑P→P′(∫0tκP→P′​(s)​c​(s)P​𝑑s)​(P′−P),c(t)=c^{0}+\sum_{P\to P^{\prime}}\left(\int_{0}^{t}\kappa_{P\to P^{\prime}}(s)c(s)^{P}ds\right)(P^{\prime}-P),

and therefore c⁡(t)∈c⁡(0)+Sc(t)\in c(0)+S for all times t≥0.t\geq 0. Moreover, it is easy to check that c⁡(t)∈ℝ≥0d;c(t)\in\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0}; indeed, all the negative terms in the expression of c˙i​(t)\dot{c}_{i}(t) coming from the right hand side of (1) contain ci​(t)c_{i}(t) as a factor and vanish on the face ci=0c_{i}=0 of ℝ≥0d.\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}. We conclude that (c0+S)∩ℝ≥0d(c^{0}+S)\cap\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d} is forward invariant for (1). Similarly one can notice that (c0+S)∩ℝ>0d(c^{0}+S)\cap\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d} is also forward invariant for (1).

2.3 Persistence and permanence of dynamical systems

We review some more vocabulary ([10, 16, 19]).

Definition 7.

A d-dimensional dynamical system is called persistent if for any forward trajectory T⁡(c0)={c⁡(t)=(x1​(t),…,xd​(t))∣t≥0}T(c_{0})=\{c(t)=(x_{1}(t),\ldots,x_{d}(t))\mid t\geq 0\} with positive initial condition c0∈ℝ>0dc_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d} we have

lim inft→∞xi​(t)>0​f​o​r​a​l​l​i∈{1,…,d}.\liminf_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)>0\ for\ all\ i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}.

Note that some authors call a dynamical system that satisfies the condition in Definition 7 strongly persistent [19]. In their work, persistence requires only that lim supt→∞xi​(t)>0\limsup_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)>0 for all i∈{1,…,d}.i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}.

Going back to Definition 7, persistence means that no forward trajectory with positive initial condition approaches the coordinate axes arbitrarily close. Note that a dynamical system with bounded trajectories is persistent if the open positive quadrant is forward invariant and there are no ω\omega-limit points on ∂ℝ≥0d;\partial\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d}; recall the definition of ω\omega-limit points below.

Definition 8.

Let T⁡(c0)={c⁡(t)∣t≥0}T(c_{0})=\{c(t)\mid t\geq 0\} denote a forward trajectory of a dynamical system with initial condition c0∈ℝ>0d.c_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d}. The ω\omega-limit set of T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) is

limωT⁡(c0)={l∈ℝd∣limn→∞c⁡(tn)=l​ for some sequence ​tn→∞}.\textstyle\lim_{\omega}T(c_{0})=\{l\in\mathbb{R}^{d}\mid\lim_{n\to\infty}c(t_{n})=l\text{ for some sequence }t_{n}\to\infty\}.

The elements of limωT⁡(c0)\lim_{\omega}T(c_{0}) are called ω\omega-limit points of T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}).

Definition 9.

A d-dimensional dynamical system is called permanent on a forward invariant set D⊆ℝ≥0dD\subseteq\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{d} if there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that for any forward trajectory T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) with positive initial condition c0∈Dc_{0}\in D we have

ϵ<lim inft→∞xi​(t)​a​n​d​lim supt→∞xi​(t)<1/ϵ​f​o​r​a​l​l​i∈{1,…,d}.\epsilon<\liminf_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)\ and\ \limsup_{t\to\infty}x_{i}(t)<1/\epsilon\ for\ all\ i\in\{1,\ldots,d\}.

In other words, a dynamical system is permanent on a forward invariant set D⊆ℝ≥0dD\subseteq\mathbb{R}^{d}_{\geq 0} if there is a compact set K⊂ℝ>0dK\subset\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{d} such that any forward trajectory with positive initial condition c0∈Dc_{0}\in D ends up in KK.

In the case of a κ\kappa-variable mass-action system, where the trajectories are confined to subspaces of ℝd,\mathbb{R}^{d}, it is meaningful to require that the system is permanent on each stoichiometric compatibility class, as we do in the following definition.

Definition 10.

A κ\kappa-variable mass-action system is called permanent if, for any stoichiometric compatibility class Σ,\Sigma, the dynamical system is permanent on Σ\Sigma.

Clearly, a permanent κ\kappa-variable mass-action system is persistent.

We therefore conclude that the mass-action system (2) is persistent. In fact, our informal discussion can be made rigorous and extended to apply to any reversible network:

Theorem 11.

Any two-species reversible κ\kappa-variable mass-action system is persistent.

Although our discussion of Theorem 11 has been informal, a rigorous proof will be given through the more general result of Theorem 17.

In the next sections we extend ideas discussed here for the case of endotactic networks which we will define soon. For reversible networks, this section revealed an important ingredient in constructing 𝒫\cal P and proving persistence. Namely, when c⁡(t)∈𝒫,c(t)\in\cal P, the aggregate effect of a pair of reversible reactions P⇌P′P\rightleftharpoons P^{\prime} is to push the trajectory towardss the corresponding Γ\Gamma region, therefore towardss the interior of 𝒫.\cal P. The “bad” reaction in P⇌P′,P\rightleftharpoons P^{\prime}, i.e. the one that points outside 𝒫\cal P is cancelled by the other, “good reaction”. Both reactions are good if c⁡(t)c(t) lies on one of the two sides parallel to P′−P.P^{\prime}-P. Which reaction is good and which is bad comes from the sign of binomials of the form

cP′−C⋅cP,c^{P^{\prime}}-C\cdot c^{P}, (4)

where CC is some positive constant, in this case C=δC=\delta or C=1/δ.C=1/\delta. Analyzing the sign of (4) for source complexes PP and P′P^{\prime} is a recurring theme throughout the paper. We will refer to this informally as “comparing source monomials up to a constant.”

4 Endotactic networks

The results we obtained in this paper are applicable to endotactic networks, a large class of two-dimensional reaction networks characterized by a simple geometric property. As we will see shortly, the class of endotactic networks is larger than the well-known class of weakly reversible networks. We build up to the definition of an endotactic network and begin with a few geometric notions.

Let ℛ=(𝒮,𝒞,ℛ,κ)\cal R=(\cal S,\cal C,\cal R,\kappa) denote a κ\kappa-variable mass-action system with two species and let 𝒮=[X,Y]{\cal S}=[X,\ Y] denote its ordered set of species.

Definition 12.

is also called the set of source complexes of ℛ.\cal R. The source monomial corresponding to (m,n)∈𝒮𝒞⁡(ℛ)(m,n)\in{\cal{SC(R)}} is xm​yn.x^{m}y^{n}.

e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)<0={P∈ℝ2∣(P−Q)⋅𝐯<0​f​o​r​a​l​l​Q∈e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)}esupp^{\bf v}({\cal R})_{<0}=\{P\in\mathbb{R}^{2}\mid(P-Q)\cdot{\bf v}<0\ for\ all\ Q\in esupp^{\bf v}({\cal R})\}

and define e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)>0esupp^{\bf v}({\cal R})_{>0} similarly.

Definition 14.

A reaction network ℛ\cal R is called endotactic if for any nonzero vector 𝐯\bf v with ℛ⊑≠Ø\cal R_{\bf v}\neq\O we have

{P→P′∣P∈e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)​ and ​P′∈e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)<0}=Ø\{P\to P^{\prime}\mid P\in esupp^{{\bf v}}({\cal R})\text{ and }P^{\prime}\in esupp^{{{\bf v}}}({\cal R})_{<0}\}=\O (5)

In other words, and perhaps more illuminating, a network is endotactic if and only if it passes the “parallel sweep test” for any nonzero vector 𝐯:\bf v: sweep the lattice plane with a line LL orthogonal to 𝐯,\bf v, going in the direction of 𝐯,\bf v, and stop when LL encounters a source complex corresponding to a reaction which is not parallel to LL. Now check that no reactions with source on LL points towards the swept region. Note that if ℛ⊑=Ø\cal R_{\bf v}=\O then LL never stops. In this case we still say that the network has passed the parallel sweep test for 𝐯.\bf v.

It is easy to verify that a reaction network is endotactic. Although, by definition, condition (5) needs to be met by any vector 𝐯,\bf v, it is easy to see that only a finite number of vectors 𝐯\bf v need to satisfy (5) in order to conclude that the network is endotactic. This fact is explained in Proposition 4.1, which we discuss next.

Let 𝐕\bf V denote the set of inward normal unit vectors to the sides of c​o​n​v​(𝒮𝒞⁡(ℛ)).conv({\cal{SC(R)}}). If c​o​n​v​(𝒮𝒞⁡(ℛ))conv({\cal{SC(R)}}) is a line segment, we consider both normal unit vectors as inward.

Using Proposition 4.1, it is straightforward to check whether a network is endotactic or not. A few examples are presented in Figure 5.

We have mentioned that the class of endotactic networks includes the class of weakly reversible networks. Indeed, this is easy to see:

Lemma 15.

Any weakly reversible reaction network is endotactic.

Proof.

In a weakly reversible network all complexes are sources, 𝒮𝒞⁡(ℛ)=𝒮.{\cal{SC(R)}}=\cal S. The definition of the essential support implies immediately that for every vector 𝐯\bf v all reactions originating on e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)esupp^{\bf v}(\cal R) point inside e​s​u​p​p𝐯​(ℛ)>0.esupp^{\bf v}({\cal R})_{>0}. ∎

Because of its relation to complex-balancing, weak reversibility is a widespread assumption in much of the work done in Chemical Reaction Network Theory ([8]). On the other hand, the results of the present paper naturally lend themselves to the much larger class of endotactic networks. In the subsequent sections we will prove persistence and permanence of endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems with two species. We conjecture that the same results are true for any number of species:

Extended Persistence Conjecture. Any endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass-action system is persistent.
Extended Permanence Conjecture. Any endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass-action55 5 Same for power-law. system is permanent.

Here “extended” refers to two different generalizations: the assumption of an endotactic, and not necessarily weakly reversible network, and for the use of the κ\kappa-variable mass-action kinetics, and not the usual mass-action kinetics, where κ\kappa is a fixed vector of parameters.

5 Construction of a forward-invariant polygon

As in the proof of persistence of the reversible example (2), our approach to proving Theorem 17 is based on defining a convex polygon 𝒫\cal P whose convex hull contains T⁡(c⁡(0))T(c(0)). Here we explain how this construction is carried out for a not necessarily reversible network.

In example (2) the aggregate effect of any two reverse reactions P⇌P′P\rightleftharpoons P^{\prime} is to drive the trajectory towards the Γ\Gamma region δ≤cP′−P≤1/δ,\delta\leq c^{P^{\prime}-P}\leq 1/\delta, therefore towards the interior of 𝒫.\cal P. In other words, the source of the “bad” reaction that might force the trajectory to cross to the exterior of 𝒫\cal P is smaller (up to some constant) than the source of the “good” reaction that keeps the trajectory in the interior of 𝒫.\cal P.

The proof of persistence for example (2) contains all the ingredients for the proof of the persistence for any two-species reversible κ\kappa-variable mass-action system. In the more general setup of a weakly reversible network, we need to adjust the setup of the invariant polygon and parts of our discussion.

In the reversible case we saw that if c⁡(t0)∈𝒫,c(t_{0})\in\cal P, every pair of reactions P⇌P′P\rightleftharpoons P^{\prime} contains a “good” reaction that dictates the overall effect of the reversible reaction. In the weakly reversible case we show that there is a “good” reaction that dictates the direction of c˙​(t0),\dot{c}(t_{0}), i.e. the aggregate effect of the whole network, up to a small enough perturbation. This amounts to showing that at time t0t_{0} with c⁡(t0)∈𝒫c(t_{0})\in\cal P there is a complex that is source to a “good” reaction and whose corresponding monomial is larger than the monomials corresponding to all other source complexes (up to some constant). This way we are led to comparing monomials cPc^{P} and cP′c^{P^{\prime}} for all pairwise combinations of source complexes PP and P′.P^{\prime}.

6 Endotactic two-species κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems: persistence and permanence

6.1 Persistence

Let (ℛ,𝒮,𝒞,κ)(\cal R,\cal S,\cal C,\kappa) denote a two-species, endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass action system with κP→P′​(t)∈(η,1/η)\kappa_{P\to P^{\prime}}(t)\in(\eta,1/\eta) for all P→P′∈ℛ.P\to P^{\prime}\in\cal R. Recall that c⁡(t)=(x⁡(t),y⁡(t))c(t)=(x(t),y(t)) denotes a solution of (1) with initial condition c⁡(0).c(0).

The following lemma is a key ingredient in the proof of Theorem 17. It states that if for some t0t_{0}, the source monomial of the reaction P0→P0′P_{0}\to P^{\prime}_{0} is larger than all other source monomials (up to a constant), then c˙​(t0)\dot{c}(t_{0}) does not deviate too far from P0′−P0.P^{\prime}_{0}-P_{0}.

Lemma 16.

Let P0→P0′∈ℛP_{0}\to P^{\prime}_{0}\in{\cal R} and let 𝐯\bf{v} be a vector such that (P0′−P0)⋅𝐯>0.(P^{\prime}_{0}-P_{0})\cdot{\bf v}>0. Lower-endotactic networks. A useful observation can be made from the proof of Theorem 17. Namely, we need not require that the network is endotactic in order to conclude that a bounded trajectory T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) is persistent. Instead, it is enough that the network is merely lower-endotactic, meaning that it passes the parallel sweep test for vectors that point inside the closed positive quadrant. Let 𝐕L{\bf V}_{L} be the set of inward normal vectors to the sides of strictly negative slope of 𝒮𝒞⁡(ℛ){\cal SC(R)} (see Proposition 4.1). In other words, a network is lower-endotactic if condition (5) is satisfied for all vectors 𝐯∈𝐕L∪{𝐢,𝐣}.{\bf v}\in{\bf V}_{L}\cup\{\bf i,\bf j\}. Indeed, we may construct the invariant polygon 𝒫\cal P such that the square [0,M]2[0,M]^{2} contains T⁡(c0).T(c_{0}). Then, if c⁡(t)c(t) reaches 𝒫,\cal P, it must be on the polygonal line [Df+1​A1​A2​…​Ae+1​B1].[D_{f+1}A_{1}A_{2}\ldots A_{e+1}B_{1}]. and the proof of (8) only requires that ℛ\cal R is lower endotactic. We cast this result as a corollary to the proof of Theorem 17.

Corollary 18.

Any bounded trajectory of a lower-endotactic κ\kappa-variable mass-action system with two species is persistent.

From (14) we obtain

which contradicts the fact that Φ⁡(c⁡(t))∈[α1,α0]\Phi(c(t))\in[\alpha_{1},\alpha_{0}] for all t≥0.t\geq 0. ∎

Remark (existence of positive equilibria for two-species autonomous endotatic mass-action systems). The existence of a positive equilibrium has been shown for weakly reversible mass-action systems in [7]. For endotactic networks we may observe that if the rate constant function depends on both time and the phase point cc, κ=κ⁡(t,c)∈(η,1/η)\kappa=\kappa(t,c)\in(\eta,1/\eta) then the set of all possible trajectories is still the same as for κ=κ⁡(t),\kappa=\kappa(t), and our persistence and permanence results still hold. In particular, if κ=κ⁡(c)∈(η,1/η)\kappa=\kappa(c)\in(\eta,1/\eta) for all c∈ℝ>02c\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{2}, then Theorem 19 together with the Brouwer Fixed Point Theorem guarantees the existence of a positive equilibrium in c​o​n​v​(𝒫⁡(α0)).conv({\cal P}(\alpha_{0})).

7 The Global Attractor Conjecture for three-species networks

As mentioned in the Introduction, the Global Attractor Conjecture concerns the asymptotic behavior of complex-balances mass-action systems and is of central importance in Chemical Reaction Network Theory.

Definition 20.

A point c∗∈ℝ≥0nc_{*}\in\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{n} of a mass-action system (ℛ,𝒮,𝒞,κ)({\cal R},{\cal S},{\cal C},\kappa) is called complex-balanced equilibrium if the aggregate flow at each complex of ℛ\cal R is zero. More precisely, for each P0∈𝒞P_{0}\in{\cal C} we have

∑P→P0κP→P0​c∗P=∑P0→PκP0→P​c∗P0.\sum_{P\to P_{0}}\kappa_{P\to P_{0}}{c_{*}}^{P}=\sum_{P_{0}\to P}\kappa_{P_{0}\to P}{c_{*}}^{P_{0}}.

A complex-balanced system is a mass-action system that admits a strictly positive complex-balanced equilibrium.

A complex-balanced system is necessarily weakly reversible [8]. A very important class of complex-balanced mass-action systems is that of weakly reversible, deficiency zero systems [8, 9]. The deficiency of a network is given by n−l−s,n-l-s, where n,n, ll and ss denote the number of complexes, the number of linkage classes and the dimension of the stoichiometric subspace. Computing the deficiency of a network is straightforward, as opposed to checking the existence of a complex-balanced equilibrium.

It is known that a complex-balanced system admits a unique positive equilibrium cΣc_{\Sigma} in each stoichiometric compatibility class Σ\Sigma and this equilibrium is complex-balanced [8]. Moreover, each such equilibrium admits a strict Lyapunov function which guarantees that cΣc_{\Sigma} is locally asymptotically stable with respect to Σ{\Sigma} [8, 12]. Recall from the Introduction that the Global Attractor Conjecture states that cΣc_{\Sigma} is in fact globally asymptotically stable with respect to Σ.{\Sigma}.

It is known that for complex-balanced mass-action systems, all trajectories with positive initial condition converge to the set of equilibria [18]. As a consequence, showing that the unique positive equilibrium cΣc_{\Sigma} in the stoichiometric compatibility class Σ\Sigma is globally attractive amounts to showing that no trajectories with positive initial conditions have ω\omega-limit points on the boundary of Σ\Sigma.

In particular, any condition that guarantees the non-existence of boundary equilibria for a stoichiometric compatibility class Σ\Sigma implies that cΣc_{\Sigma} is globally attractive. For instance, it was shown that a face FF of Σ\Sigma contains boundary equilibria only if the species corresponding to coordinates that vanish on FF form a semilocking set (siphon in Petri nets terminology) [3, 1, 2]. It follows that if no face of Σ\Sigma corresponds to a semilocking set then Σ\Sigma does not have boundary equilibria and cΣc_{\Sigma} is globally attractive. Algebraic methods for computing siphons have been devised in [17].

Some progress has been made for the remaining case where boundary equilibria cannot be ruled out. It was shown that ω\omega-limit points cannot be vertices of Σ\Sigma [5, 1] and that codimension-one faces of Σ\Sigma are “repelling” [2]. As a consequence, the Gobal Attractor Conjecture holds for systems with two-dimensional stoichiometric subspace [2]. For systems with three-dimensional and higher-dimensional stoichiometric subspace the conjecture is open. In particular, previous results do not apply to the general three-species systems. In what follows we show the conjecture to be true in this case.

Theorem 21.

The Global Attractor Conjecture holds for three-species networks.

Proof.

Let (𝒮,𝒞,ℛ,κ)(\cal S,\cal C,\cal R,\kappa) denote a complex-balanced reaction system with ordered set of species {X,Y,Z}\{X,Y,Z\} and denote the corresponding concentration vector at time tt by c⁡(t)=(x⁡(t),y⁡(t),z⁡(t)).c(t)=(x(t),y(t),z(t)). Let c0∈ℝ>03c_{0}\in\mathbb{R}_{>0}^{3} be arbitrary and let T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) denote the forward trajectory of the concentration vector with initial condition c0.c_{0}. We want to prove that T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) converges to the unique positive equilibrium in the stoichiometric compatibility class of c0.c_{0}.

The existence of the Lyapunov function guarantees, on one hand, that there is a neighborhood of the origin that is not visited by T⁡(c0),T(c_{0}), and on the other hand, that T⁡(c0)T(c_{0}) is bounded [5, 1]. In other words, there exists ϵ>0\epsilon>0 such that x⁡(t)+y⁡(t)+z⁡(t)>3​ϵx(t)+y(t)+z(t)>3\epsilon and x⁡(t),y⁡(t)x(t),\ y(t) and z⁡(t)z(t) are all smaller than 1/ϵ1/\epsilon at all times t≥0.t\geq 0.

8 Examples

8.1 Thomas-type models

The Thomas mechanism (see [13, ch. 6]) is a substrate inhibition model for a specific reaction involving oxygen and uric acid in the presence of the enzyme uricase. After nondimensionalization the ODEs for oxygen (v)(v) and uric acid (u)(u) become

d​ud​t=a−u−T⁡(u,v)​u​v,\displaystyle\frac{du}{dt}=a-u-T(u,v)uv, (25)
d​vd​t=α⁡(b−v)−T⁡(u,v)​u​v,\displaystyle\frac{dv}{dt}=\alpha(b-v)-T(u,v)uv,

where in the Thomas model T⁡(u,v)=ρ​(1+u+K​u2)−1.T(u,v)=\rho(1+u+Ku^{2})^{-1}. Here all parameters a,b,α,ρa,b,\alpha,\rho and KK are positive. Using Theorem 19 we can show that (25) is permanent for any function T⁡(u,v)≥0T(u,v)\geq 0 that is continuous and does not vanish on a compact K⊃[0,a]×[0,b]K\supset[0,a]\times[0,b] (in particular, this is true for function TT in the Thomas mechanism). Indeed, for some time point t0t_{0} we have (u⁡(t),v⁡(t))∈K;(u(t),v(t))\in K; continuity of TT guarantees that for t≥t0t\geq t_{0} we have η<T⁡(u⁡(t),v⁡(t))<1/η\eta<T(u(t),v(t))<1/\eta for some η>0.\eta>0. The dynamical system (25) can be written as a κ\kappa-variable mass-action system with reactions given in Figure 10 (a), where the reaction rates are specified on the reaction arrows and T⁡(t)=T⁡(u⁡(t),v⁡(t)).T(t)=T(u(t),v(t)). This network is endotactic and Theorem 19 implies that the dynamical system (25) is permanent.

8.2 Power-law systems

In the proof of Theorem 17 we have not used the fact that the exponents PP of monomials cPc^{P} in (1) are nonnegative integers; this is the case when P⊂ℤ≥02P\subset\mathbb{Z}_{\geq 0}^{2} represents a chemical complex, which has been our framework thus far. In fact, the proof of Theorem 17 accommodates the case when P⊂ℝ2P\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} has any real components.

More precisely, keeping the notation c⁡(t)=(x⁡(t),y⁡(t)),c(t)=(x(t),y(t)), we consider an ODE system of the following form:

c˙​(t)=∑P∈𝒮𝒞∑𝐯∈V⁡(P)κP,𝐯​(t)​cP​𝐯\dot{c}(t)=\sum_{P\in{\cal{SC}}}\sum_{{\bf v}\in V(P)}\kappa_{P,{\bf v}}(t)c^{P}{\bf v} (26)

where 𝒮𝒞⊂ℝ2{\cal{SC}}\subset\mathbb{R}^{2} is the set of “sources” PP and V⁡(P)V(P) is the set of “reaction vectors” with source P.P. We also suppose that κP,𝐯​(t)∈(η,1/η)\kappa_{P,{\bf v}}(t)\in(\eta,1/\eta) for some 0<η<1.0<\eta<1. With this interpretation, (26) is a generalization of a κ\kappa-variable mass-action ODE system (1) and Theorems 17 and 19 still apply.

A particularly important example of power-law, not necessarily polynomial systems is the class of S-systems ([15]), where each component of the right hand side of (26) consists of a difference of two “generalized monomials” (i.e., monomials with real exponents). S-systems are common in the modeling of metabolic and genetic networks. For example, consider the following S-system:

d​xd​t=2​x−1​y1.5−y0.8\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt}=2x^{-1}y^{1.5}-y^{0.8} (27)
d​yd​t=y−2−5​x−1​y1.5\displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt}=y^{-2}-\sqrt{5}x^{-1}y^{1.5}

Note that it is not obvious that trajectories of (27) cannot reach ∂ℝ≥02\partial\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{2} in finite time. However, using Theorem 19 we can easily see that (27) is in fact permanent, and, in particular, all trajectories with positive initial condition will be bounded away from zero and infinity. Indeed, the generalized monomials in (27), i.e. the points (−1,1.5),(0,0.8)(-1,1.5),(0,0.8) and (0,−2),(0,-2), as well as the corresponding “reaction vectors” (2,−5),(−1,0)(2,-\sqrt{5}),(-1,0) and (0,1)(0,1) are illustrated in Figure 10 (b). This configuration is endotactic and Theorem 19 applies.

Note that the same conclusion holds for any system of the form

d​xd​t=2​κ1​(t)​x−1​y1.5−κ2​(t)​y0.8\displaystyle\frac{dx}{dt}=2\kappa_{1}(t)x^{-1}y^{1.5}-\kappa_{2}(t)y^{0.8} (28)
d​yd​t=κ3​(t)​y−2−5​κ1​(t)​x−1​y1.5\displaystyle\frac{dy}{dt}=\kappa_{3}(t)y^{-2}-\sqrt{5}\kappa_{1}(t)x^{-1}y^{1.5}

where κi​(t)∈(η,1/η)\kappa_{i}(t)\in(\eta,1/\eta) for all i∈{1,2,3}i\in\{1,2,3\} and for all t≥0.t\geq 0.

8.3 Lotka-Volterra systems

The classical two-species predator-prey model

A→2​AA+B→2​BB→0A\to 2A\quad A+B\to 2B\quad B\to 0 (29)

is neither endotactic nor lower endotactic. Since, for fixed parameters its trajectories are either constant or closed orbits, the system is not permanent (see Figure 10 (c)). On the other hand, the fixed-parameter system has bounded trajectories and is persistent, which seems to suggest that the requirement of entotactic network may be weakened in Corollary 18. Note, however, that the result of the corollary concerns κ\kappa-variable mass-action systems. It is not hard to show that, in general, the κ\kappa-variable Lotka-Volterra system (29) is not persistent.

8.4 Examples for the three-species Global Attractor Conjecture

We present two examples of reaction networks for which no previously known results can resolve the question of global asymptotic stability, but for which Theorem 21 applies.

(30)

The first example, given by (30) (a) is Example 5.4 from [2]; it is reversible with one linkage class. On the other hand, example (30) (b) is weakly-reversible, but not reversible and has two linkage classes. Moreover, the deficiency of both networks is zero and therefore the two mass-action systems are complex-balanced.

In both examples all stoichiometric compatibility classes are equal to ℝ≥03.\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{3}. If (x⁡(t),y⁡(t),z⁡(t))(x(t),y(t),z(t)) denotes the concentrations of (A,B,C),(A,B,C), then it is easy to see that all points on the nonnegative zz axis are equilibria for both examples. Therefore boundary equilibria exist, and moreover, except for the origin, they all lie on a codimension-two face of ℝ≥03.\mathbb{R}_{\geq 0}^{3}. In this case all previously known results stay silent, but Theorem 21 guarantees that, in each example, the unique positive equilibrium is globally asymptotically stable.
